questions.brief: This React component should increase the count on click and show the count in the title, but it is buggy. Which fix is correct?
options: Change `let count = 0` to `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)` and `onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}`
Move `let count = 0` outside the component function
questions.explanation: React requires `useState` to track state changes and trigger a re-render. A local variable like `let count` will not update the UI when changed.

questions.brief: What does this do? `useEffect(() => { loadUser(id); }, [id]);`
options: It runs only once, when the app first loads
It runs after every single render
It runs after the first render and again whenever `id` changes
It runs before the component renders
questions.explanation: The dependency array `[id]` tells React to re-run the effect only when `id` changes, plus once after the first render.

questions.brief: A login form sends a password from the browser to your API. What is the minimum you must do?
options: Send it over HTTPS and store only a salted hash (bcrypt or argon2) on the server
Encode it with base64 before sending
Store the password in localStorage so the user stays logged in
Hash it with MD5 in the browser and store that
questions.explanation: HTTPS protects it in transit, and a slow salted hash (bcrypt/argon2) protects it at rest. Base64 is not encryption and MD5 is far too fast.

questions.brief: You need to design a `POST /orders` endpoint for an e-commerce shop. Which of the following is the best practice for the response status code upon successful creation?
questions.explanation: The 201 Created status code is the HTTP standard for a successful POST request that results in the creation of a new resource.

questions.brief: Which index speeds up `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42` the most?
options: No index is needed, SQL is always fast
questions.explanation: An index on the column you filter by lets the database jump to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table.

questions.brief: Two customers try to buy the last item at the same moment. What prevents overselling?
options: Checking the stock in the browser first
Running the update in a transaction, using a row lock or an atomic `UPDATE ... WHERE stock > 0`
questions.explanation: Concurrency bugs need the database to enforce the rule atomically. Browser checks and bigger servers don't remove the race.

questions.brief: A login form has a password field requiring 8-20 characters. Which of the following test inputs is the best example of 'Boundary Value Analysis'?
options: A password with special characters like !@#$
Leaving the password field completely empty
questions.explanation: Boundary Value Analysis tests the exact boundaries (8 and 20) and the values just outside them (7 and 21) to catch off-by-one errors.

questions.brief: A field accepts ages from 18 to 60. Which set of test values best covers the boundaries?
questions.explanation: Boundary testing checks just outside and exactly on each edge: 17 and 18 at the bottom, 60 and 61 at the top.

questions.brief: In the testing pyramid, which kind of test should you have the FEWEST of?
questions.explanation: End-to-end tests are the slowest and most fragile, so you keep a small number for critical journeys and rely on many fast unit tests.

questions.brief: You have an `orders` table with `customer_id` and `amount`. You need to find the total revenue per customer. Which SQL clause must you use?
questions.explanation: The `GROUP BY` clause is used alongside aggregate functions like `SUM(amount)` to group the result set by one or more columns (e.g., customer_id).

questions.brief: Which query gives the number of orders per customer?
options: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id;`
`SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;`
questions.explanation: `GROUP BY customer_id` makes one row per customer, and `COUNT(*)` counts the orders in each group.

questions.brief: Sales dropped 20% in March. What should you check FIRST before reporting it?
options: Whether the data is complete and comparable (missing days, tracking changes, fewer working days)
Whether you can remove March from the chart
questions.explanation: A sudden drop is often a data problem (missing days, broken tracking) rather than a real change, so verify the data first.

questions.brief: You are writing a Dockerfile for a Node.js app. Which of the following correctly installs the production dependencies?
questions.explanation: `npm ci --only=production` is the best practice for CI and Docker builds because it strictly follows the package-lock.json and skips devDependencies.

questions.brief: A new release breaks production. What is the fastest SAFE fix?
options: Debug directly on the production server
Roll back to the previous known-good version
Restart every server again and again
Delete the logs so nobody sees the errors
questions.explanation: Rolling back restores service quickly and safely. You then debug the failed release calmly in a non-production environment.

questions.brief: What is the main purpose of a CI pipeline?
options: To deploy to production without running tests
To automatically build and test every change so problems are found early
questions.explanation: CI runs the build and tests on every change, so breakages are caught within minutes instead of days later.

questions.brief: A college wants a chatbot that answers ONLY from its 200-page rules PDF. To prevent hallucination, what is the most critical step in your RAG pipeline?
options: Use a larger LLM like GPT-4 instead of a smaller one
Instruct the LLM in the prompt to 'only use the provided context and say I don't know if the answer is missing'
Increase the temperature of the LLM to 1.0
Generate embeddings for the entire 200-page PDF as a single chunk
questions.explanation: Prompt constraints are crucial in RAG. Explicitly telling the model to rely solely on the retrieved context and admit ignorance prevents it from falling back on its training data (hallucinating).

questions.brief: In a RAG system, what happens when a user asks a question?
options: The model is retrained on the question
The most relevant text chunks are retrieved and placed in the prompt, then the model answers
The model is compressed to answer faster
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant chunks from your documents at question time and gives them to the model as context. No retraining is involved.

questions.brief: Which setup most directly reduces made-up answers in a document Q&A bot?
options: Raise the temperature so answers are more creative
Answer only from retrieved text, cite the source, and say "I don't know" when nothing relevant is found
questions.explanation: Grounding answers in retrieved text and allowing "I don't know" is the most direct protection against hallucination.

questions.brief: A customer writes: 'Your API returns 401 since this morning and my shop is down!'. What is the most likely technical cause of a 401 error?
options: The server is completely down and offline
The customer's API key is missing, expired, or invalid
The customer is sending invalid JSON in the request body
The endpoint URL was mistyped (e.g., /apii instead of /api)
questions.explanation: 401 Unauthorized specifically means the request lacks valid authentication credentials. 400 is for invalid JSON, 404 is for mistyped URLs, and 50x is for server downtime.

questions.brief: A customer writes "it doesn't work". What is the best first reply?
options: Tell them to reinstall the app
Ask for the exact steps, what they expected, what happened instead, and any error message
Say it works fine on your machine
questions.explanation: You can't fix what you can't reproduce. Clear steps, expected vs actual behaviour, and the error message give you what you need.

questions.brief: An API call returns HTTP 403. What does that usually mean?
options: The request body is not valid JSON
You are identified, but you are not allowed to do that
questions.explanation: 401 means "who are you?" (not authenticated) while 403 means "I know who you are, but you may not do this" (not authorised).

questions.brief: Given an array of numbers, the brute force Two Sum solution (nested loops) has a time complexity of O(n^2). By using a Hash Map, you can optimize this. What is the time complexity of the Hash Map solution?
questions.explanation: A Hash Map allows O(1) lookups. By passing through the array once and storing/checking values in the map, the overall time complexity drops to O(n).

questions.brief: Which data structure gives O(1) average-time lookup by key?
options: A sorted array with binary search
questions.explanation: Hash maps compute a slot from the key, so lookup is O(1) on average. Binary search and balanced trees are O(log n), linked lists O(n).

questions.brief: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n items?
questions.explanation: Each step halves the remaining range, so it takes about log2(n) steps.

questions.brief: In React Native, which component should render a long scrollable list efficiently?
options: `ScrollView` with every item mapped inside it
questions.explanation: `FlatList` renders only the items near the screen and recycles them, which keeps long lists smooth and memory-friendly.

questions.brief: A mobile app must stay useful on a train with no signal. Which approach helps most?
options: Cache data locally and sync when the connection returns
Show a loading spinner until the network is back
Ask the user to log in again each time
questions.explanation: Offline-first apps read from a local cache and sync later, so users keep working without a connection.

questions.brief: Where should an app store a user's authentication token?
options: In plain text in a file
In the operating system's secure storage (iOS Keychain / Android Keystore)
In the URL so it is easy to share
questions.explanation: Keychain and Keystore are encrypted, OS-protected storage. Plain files and source code can be read by others.
